title: Ed Reform Is Dead — it’s Parent Choice or Public Schools
author: Benjamin Riley and James Shanahan
summary: Benjamin Riley and James Shanahan argue that the early 2000s education reform consensus of test-based accountability, achievement gaps and choice plus accountability is not coming back, because both political wings have moved on. They retell the history to show that conservatives themselves undermined No Child Left Behind, the Common Core and standardised testing, so there is no reason for them to return to those policies. The new right-wing goal, they say, is parent choice through Education Savings Accounts, driven by the principle that parents are the primary educators and by religious motivation rather than competition or achievement, with the state stepping back from asking whether children learn. On the left, they argue that parents want their public schools back and are organising against ed tech and AI, so the centre-left ed reformers' choice plus accountability has no audience. They conclude that the real contest is between parent choice and defending public schools, and urge readers to vote and to engage in school board elections.
points: The authors argue that ed-reform nostalgia rests on a misremembered history in which Republicans and suburban opt-out parents helped dismantle accountability and the Common Core.

Parent choice differs from school choice because public money goes to parents for tuition, microschooling, homeschool materials and tutoring, and the state no longer has a stake in whether children learn.
They claim the movement is motivated by parental rights and faith rather than market competition, citing the Garnetts' and John Coons's writing.
Documented ESA misuse and Florida's loss of track of 30,000 voucher recipients are presented as evidence that accountability is no longer a priority on the right.
On the left they see parents mobilising for public schools and against screens and AI, so they predict choice plus accountability will find no political home.
quotes: Something strange is happening in education politics in the United States. A tectonic political shift has occured, and public education may collapse as a result.

But as a general matter, ed reform is not coming back, and we think these pundits are all making the same basic mistake. Whether through ignorance or willful blindness, they are failing to grasp just how dramatically the education political landscape in America has shifted on both the right and the left.

Conservatives fought to end No Child Left Behind. Conservatives rejected the Common Core. Conservatives opted their children out of standardized tests. Why would they come back to the table now for a do-over of classic ed-reform policies?
The answer is that the right has quietly been building an intellectual ecosystem to advance parent choice via Education Savings Accounts, with the aim of hollowing out public education entirely.

Under parent choice, whether children learn is simply not the state’s concern. Parents decide whether their children lean, if they choose to care about this at all. But policy-wise, once public money is in parental hands, the state’s role in education is finished.

Instead, what parents on the left really want is their public schools back, the ones they remember happily attending in their childhood before ed reform was a thing, with teachers who didn’t have to spend months on test prep, and in classrooms that hadn’t been ravaged by Big Tech and other ed-tech intrusions.

The ed-reform agenda severely weakened public schooling in America, the right is moving in for the kill, and so now the left must do what it has so often done in this country’s history, however imperfectly — organize and fight for social justice.
